passage: Bao read Nadia's barter plan twice and said only, "It's a nice idea, but nobody has tried it." Nadia was stung for a minute, then opened her notebook. She did not drop the idea. Instead she picked one lane, the one with fourteen doors, and told the neighbours she would run it for two weeks. A shared shelf by the corner shop held parcels, and a paper sheet listed favours on offer. By day six people used the shelf happily, but nobody signed the favour sheet. Neighbours said writing favours down felt like keeping accounts. On day ten Nadia swapped the sheet for a thank-you jar and a weekly chat over tea. At the end she wrote down what people accepted and what they had not, and began planning the next lane.

passage:
At the co-working space in Jayanagar, Neelam sat across from Dhruv, the mentor from the startup programme, with her barter delivery pitch open on the laptop.
"It's an interesting idea," Dhruv said. "But you have no evidence anyone will carry a stranger's parcel. Test it before you build anything."
Neelam's first instinct was to argue. Instead, she closed the pitch deck. "Okay. One lane. Two weeks."
She chose 4th Cross, where she already knew six families. She made a paper sign-up sheet and a simple phone list. Each evening she noted who asked for help, who carried, and what went wrong.
After two weeks she came back. "People happily carry medicines and vegetables for neighbours they know. Nobody wanted to carry parcels for strangers. And three families wanted to pay a small fee instead of owing a favour."
Dhruv nodded. "So now you know what the idea actually is."

qa.q: Which lane did Neelam choose for the trial?
qa.a: She chose 4th Cross, where she already knew six families.

qa.q: How might Neelam have felt when Dhruv said she had no evidence?
qa.a: She probably felt defensive at first, since her instinct was to argue, but then open enough to test it.

qa.q: What else could Neelam test next, and why?
qa.a: She could try a small fee option in a second lane, since three families preferred paying to owing favours.

qa.q: How does Dhruv see Neelam's trial results?
qa.a: Dhruv is pleased, seeing that she now knows what the idea really is instead of guessing.

grounding: It shows a young founder told her barter idea is untested, running a two-week trial in one lane and adjusting the idea from what she learns.

passage:
Dear Gargi,
You were right, and I want to tell you how.
When I pitched the book-barter idea at your workshop in June, you said the reframe was clever but untested, and asked what the smallest test would be. I was a bit stung. I had already planned an app.
Instead, I picked one lane in our colony, Lane 3, with twenty-two houses. For two weeks I put a shelf outside my gate and a notebook beside it: take a book, leave a book, write your name.
Here's what I learned. People loved leaving books. Only a few took any. Children's books vanished in a day, novels sat untouched. And nobody wrote their name, so trust wasn't the problem I thought it was.
So I've changed the idea. It's now a children's book shelf, restocked by donations, in three lanes. Still no app.
Thank you for asking that one question.
Parveen

qa.q: How many houses were in Lane 3?
How did Parveen feel when Gargi called the idea untested?
qa.a: Parveen felt a bit stung at first, having already planned an app.

qa.q: What else could Parveen test in the three new lanes, and why?
qa.a: Parveen could track how many children's books go out each week in each lane, to see if the shelves keep being used after the first rush.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Gargi may feel pleased and proud that a single question led to a real test and a better idea.

grounding: It shows a young founder testing a reframed barter idea with a two-week trial in one lane and adjusting it from what people actually did.
